claims.text: The starting material is a homogenized, single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy such as CoCrFeMnNi.
The intervention uses a 1–5 at% addition of Nb or Ta.
Aging an Nb- or Ta-modified FCC HEA will induce nanoscale precipitate formation.
The resulting precipitates will be Nb-rich or Ta-rich phases dispersed within the FCC matrix.
Controlled nanoscale precipitation will improve the combined strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance relative to a single-phase FCC HEA.
Precipitate strengthening will increase yield strength.
Nanoscale precipitation will increase Young’s modulus.
Fine precipitates impede dislocation motion.
Retention of the FCC matrix will prevent a substantial loss of ductility.
Suppressing coarse grain-boundary precipitation will preserve fracture resistance.
Yield strength will increase by more than 20% relative to the baseline FCC HEA.
Young’s modulus will increase by more than 20% relative to the baseline FCC HEA.
Elongation to failure will exceed 30%.
Fracture toughness will exceed 80 MPa√m.
The representative single-phase FCC baseline has a yield strength of approximately 400 MPa.
The representative single-phase FCC baseline has an elongation of approximately 40%.
The representative single-phase FCC baseline has a Young’s modulus of approximately 200 GPa.
The representative single-phase FCC baseline has a fracture toughness of approximately 70 MPa√m.
The hypothesized benefit may fail when precipitate size exceeds 100 nm because of coarsening.
Destabilization of the FCC matrix or formation of brittle intermetallics may eliminate the proposed mechanical-property benefit.

contradictions.description: Ductility is said to be maintained or improved relative to a baseline elongation of approximately 40%, but the example success criterion is only elongation greater than 30%, which permits a substantial reduction.
